title: Technical deep dive: performance + guardrails (moderation placement)
summary: Deep dive on how safety/moderation filters impact runtime performance; discussed placement options (pre-inference, in-model, post-inference, async), caching strategies, batching and KV cache interactions, quantization effects, VPC/on-prem constraints, and proposed benchmark plan and POC next steps.
topics: KV cache and prefix-level safety checks
quantization effects on safety model accuracy
action_items: Priya Nair: run microbenchmarks comparing pre-filter (CPU) vs post-filter (GPU) on 1k sample prompts - due 2025-10-22
Alex Martin: provide representative prompt set and traffic profile - due 2025-10-20
Jordan Lee: share Redwood security and moderation docs + suggested config snippets - due 2025-10-17
next_steps: Redwood to run benchmark with moderation as pre-filter on CPU and async post-filter on GPU and share p50/p95/p99 and throughput numbers
Customer to provide sample prompt corpus and high-priority safety categories
Schedule follow-up to review benchmarks and pick placement approach (target 2025-10-24)
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-10-15 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Sam Torres (Redwood SE), Alex Martin (BrightPath Head of ML), Priya Gomez (BrightPath Security), Daniel Cho (BrightPath Infra), Maya Ruiz (Product)

[00:00] Jordan: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a deep dive on safety filters and how they affect runtime, trying to keep this practical for your POC and on-prem plans
[00:18] Alex: yeah thanks, we've got concerns about p95 latency if we add heavy moderation, and also how that fits with our VPC/on-prem box constraints
[00:32] Priya (Redwood): cool, so high-level we typically consider three placements: pre-inference classifier (fast), in-model guardrails (via prompts/structures), and post-inference moderation. each has diffs in latency and cost
[00:47] Priya (Redwood): quick note transcription, sorry, um, i might say KV cache but sometimes the tool transcribed it as K-V cat, so please excuse small typos
[01:05] Sam: i'll kick off with some numbers we generally see: a lightweight CPU-based pre-filter can run ~0.5-3ms per request depending on model and text length, so p95 tends to be small. a heavy neural classifier (100M+) on CPU jumps to 20-80ms; on GPU it's <10ms but then you pay GPU cycles and scheduling overhead
[01:30] Daniel: what about batching? our main use is chat, so smaller batches more frequent, we worry about batching adding latency
[01:45] Priya (Redwood): yes batching helps throughput but increases tail latency. for moderation pre-filters we often don't batch (stateless fast rule-based or small NN) to keep p95 low. for async pipelines you can batch post-filters to amortize cost
[02:12] Alex: can you explain prefix-level safety? we heard about short-circuiting generation if unsafe early
[02:26] Priya (Redwood): sure — prefix-level checks mean you run a safety check on the prompt or early tokens (or use a fast classifier on prefixes) and if it's flagged, you short-circuit before heavy generation. this leverages KV cache because you avoid populating long kv cache sequences for bad requests
[02:50] Maya (Customer): oh interesting — so that lowers GPU token compute because those requests never make it to the expensive stage
[03:05] Priya (Redwood): exactly. tradeoff is false positives if classifier too conservative. that's where we recommend a cascaded approach: quick rule-based filter -> fast NN pre-filter -> model-level soft guardrails -> post-check for high-risk outputs
[03:28] Alex: how do quantized models play into this? does lower precision change moderation accuracy if we run moderation models on quantized GPUs?
[03:42] Sam: good question. quantization impacts model fidelity — for classification moderations EE we test 8-bit quantized small classifiers and see small drops in accuracy (1-3%), but it's workload dependent. for safety-critical categories that matters. sometimes we run moderation on separate higher-precision hosts or keep safety models unquantized and only quantize text gen model
[04:10] Priya (Redwood): also note that running safety checks in the same GPU inference pool as the generator can cause interference: KV cache eviction, memory pressure, context switching. best practice is to offload safety classifier to CPU pool or dedicated smaller GPU pool if you need low-latency GPU classifier
[04:35] Daniel: in our on-prem setup we have limited GPU capacity. what are your recommendations for VPC/on-prem constraints?
[04:47] Priya (Redwood): for on-prem with limited GPUs we usually recommend: prefer pre-filter on CPU or tiny edge devices; reserve GPUs for generation; if you must run GPU classifiers, schedule them on separate inference nodes with smaller batch sizes and prioritize throughput/latency via QoS. Redwood Dedicated also supports reserving small GPU pools for classifiers to avoid evicting gen workloads
[05:12] Alex: curious about caching — if we cache moderation results keyed by prompt hash, how often is that valid? user prompts vary a lot
[05:25] Priya (Redwood): caching helps for repeated prompts or system prompts. for dynamic user content caching has limited hit rate, but you can cache based on normalized prompt templates or prefix hashes. caution: caching must respect TTLs and versioning when your safety rules/models update
[05:47] Jordan: also for embeddings-based semantic checks sometimes we precompute embeddings for known bad patterns and do a nearest-neighbor check at request time — that can be cheap if your ANN index is on CPU and hits are managed
[06:05] Priya Gomez (Customer): how about async moderation? we could let generator return, then retroactively moderate and redact, but we worry about UX liabilities if unsafe content is sent then retracted
[06:21] Priya (Redwood): yep async reduces latency but increases UX/legal risk. some customers send a confidence label and include uncertain content behind a 'needs review' flow. others send token-granular redactions. For healthcare use-cases it's risky to allow any potentially harmful content to reach users without synchronous checks
[06:44] Maya (Customer): we are regulated, so sync checks might be required for certain categories. do you support per-route policies?
[06:53] Priya (Redwood): yes, per-route policies are supported. you can mark routes as 'high risk' and force sync pre-filters; lower-risk routes can use async checks and post-moderation
[07:08] Sam: another trick — partial generation: generate a short prefix (e.g., 32 tokens), run a mid-generation safety filter on the prefix, then continue. that reduces wasted generation compute when unsafe and keeps latency reasonable because the mid-check is fast and can be batched across requests
[07:36] Alex: what about instrumentation — how will we measure overhead and regressions?
[07:43] Jordan: Redwood Console gives token-level latency breakdown, per-route p95s, and traces for filter steps. for the POC we'll show delta with and without moderator in same workload to isolate overheads
[08:05] Daniel: any notes on rate-limiting /burst when moderation runs on CPU? could CPU become the bottleneck when you scale?
[08:15] Priya (Redwood): yep that's common. CPU pre-filters scale differently; you need autoscaling rules for CPU-based filter services. we suggest autoscaling based on queue latency and request rate and configure burst capacity (or circuit-break to fail-safe to post-filter)
[08:39] Alex: you mentioned circuit-breakers and graceful degradation earlier, can you elaborate?
[08:47] Priya (Redwood): if CPU moderation is saturated, we recommend fallback policies: route to a simpler rule-based filter (less accurate but fast), or degrade to post-hoc moderation with response labeled 'pending review', or route to a lower-capacity dedicated GPU pool. the choice depends on risk appetite
[09:10] Jordan: let's talk numbers for a sample profile: assume avg prompt 120 tokens, generation 80 tokens, tokenization overhead etc. with pre-filter CPU (light) we saw ~50ms median and 120ms p95; with heavy GPU classifier pre-filter it's 80ms median and 200ms p95 because of scheduling; post-filter async keeps generation p95 low but end-to-end detection delayed
[09:44] Sam: throughput wise batching on generator is huge: 4-8x improvement for token throughput when you can batch 8-16 requests. but moderation often can't be batched the same way if it's per-request and low-latency, so you need to architect two pipelines
[10:03] Maya (Customer): ok how does KV cache interact? if we short-circuit early we don't fill KV cache, that helps memory and throughput right?
[10:13] Priya (Redwood): right — avoiding unnecessary KV cache population saves memory and reduces future eviction churn. also for multi-turn chat you can cache safety verdicts per conversation id/prompt prefix to avoid re-checking frequently repeated system prompts
[10:31] Alex: is there tooling to simulate worst-case tail latency caused by moderation?
[10:37] Jordan: yes we can simulate with Redwood benchmarks: load generator with mixed routes, vary filter latencies, and produce p50/p95/p99 traces. we'll include KV cache cold vs warm runs to show differences
[10:56] Priya (Redwood): another nuance: moderation models can be smaller than gen models — e.g., tiny 30M classifier that runs fast but lower quality. cascades help: small model -> medium model -> flag for human review if uncertain
[11:12] Daniel: curious, does quantization of the generator model ever affect the safety post-checks that analyze generated tokens? it's more about generator output quality than moderation accuracy right
[11:23] Sam: mostly yes — quantized generators may produce slightly different tokens, which could change downstream moderation detection. but in practice we saw only minor variance; still include gen model quantization as a variable in tests
[11:41] Alex: let's walk through an example flow you propose for our on-prem POC with limited GPUs
[11:49] Priya (Redwood): recommended flow: 1) Route all requests to redwood edge controller in your VPC; 2) Run lightweight rule-based pre-filter on CPU (regex, known-bad hash); 3) If rule-based passes, run small NN pre-filter on separate CPU pool or tiny GPU if latency budget allows; 4) If pre-filter passes, send to quantized generator on GPU; 5) Optionally do async post-filtering for low-risk routes; 6) For high-risk routes, force synchronous higher-precision GPU classifier or human review
[12:23] Maya: that sounds reasonable. what about audit logs and evidence for flagged items? we need to store verdicts and anonymized contexts
[12:34] Jordan: Redwood stores moderation events with redacted context on request, supports integration with customer KMS for encryption of logs, and you can configure retention and export for audits. we'll share our security doc
[12:52] Priya Gomez: how much overhead does logging add? if we log every token that's insane
[12:58] Priya (Redwood): typically we log event-level metadata: request id, route, verdict, confidence, blackbox link to stored redacted payload. logging is async and batched to minimize latency
[13:18] Alex: any gotchas on model versioning and moderation? if you update the safety model or generator, cached results may be invalid
[13:27] Sam: yes you must tag cache entries with model and policy version; Redwood supports versioned caching and invalidation hooks when you roll a new safety policy or model
[13:44] Jordan: ok let's talk about the POC metrics: we will measure generator p50/p95/p99, moderation p50/p95, total end-to-end for sync flows, throughput (tokens/s), and cost delta. also measure false positive/negative rates on your sample corpus
[14:05] Alex: sounds good. what about false positives on prefix-level short-circuit? worried about UX impact
[14:13] Priya (Redwood): tune classifier threshold differently for prefix checks — prefer higher recall in final checks but for prefix try higher precision to avoid false positives. cascade reduces harm
[14:28] Daniel: can we use embeddings similarity as a cheap pre-check?
[14:33] Sam: yes approximate nearest neighbor on embeddings can flag semantic matches quickly; it's CPU-friendly and good for known bad templates
[14:45] Alex: any examples from other customers?
[14:49] Jordan: some regulated customers run a two-tier: synchronous light-filter + delayed full moderation for human review. others with high throughput use a split path where critical routes enforce sync checks and low-risk routes default to async. we can anonymize benchmarks for you
[15:05] Priya Gomez: ok, logistics — we need to understand the p95 target. for our product we want p95 < 300ms for end-to-end on high-priority routes. is that achievable with sync moderation?
[15:19] Priya (Redwood): yes but it'll constrain your choices: keep pre-filters lightweight, avoid GPU-based classifiers in the hot path, optimize batching for generator, and possibly increase reserved capacity. we can get near 200-300ms p95 with the right config and hardware
[15:38] Alex: if we had to pick one quick win what would it be?
[15:41] Priya (Redwood): implement a cascaded pre-filter and cache normalized prompts; that buys most wins without major infra changes
[16:00] Jordan: let's outline the benchmark plan now — Priya will run three configs: (A) no moderation, (B) lightweight pre-filter (rules + tiny NN on CPU), (C) sync GPU classifier pre-filter. we'll measure p50/p95/p99 and throughput and also measure KV cache warm/cold
[16:21] Priya (Redwood): and we'll include an async post-filter scenario for comparison
[16:27] Alex: will Redwood share scripts or harness to run locally in our VPC?
[16:33] Jordan: yes we can share a benchmark harness and docker compose for on-prem sim, plus suggested instance types and config. Sam: we'll also include sample scripts to normalize prompts for caching experiments
[16:49] Maya: one more question — regulatory evidence: do you retain full text for audit or can we configure redaction?
[16:58] Jordan: configurable. we support redaction and pseudonymization, plus export hooks to your audit pipeline with KMS encryption
[17:10] Priya Gomez: ok, timelines — we want initial results within a week
[17:15] Jordan: we'll aim to deliver the first benchmark results by 2025-10-22
[17:23] Alex: thanks, any closing notes?
[17:27] Priya (Redwood): just one more thought: consider model ensembles for high-risk categories — e.g., require agreement across two small classifiers to reduce false positives/negatives; adds compute but cheap compared to human review costs
[17:45] Jordan: cool i'll capture action items. thanks everyone
[17:52] Alex: thanks all
[18:00] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-attribution and minor word errors; timestamps are approximate and inserted for readability.
